b: This passage comes from the darkest setting in Lamentations, yet it shines with the gentlest light. Amid desolation and tears, Jeremiah saw that God’s faithfulness remained. Although everything seemed destroyed, he declared, “It is of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed.” This is the eyes of faith: seeing God’s grace even in pain.

God’s mercy is not an occasional comfort but a practical supply renewed every day. “They are new every morning” reminds us that however dark yesterday was, God’s faithfulness is still in effect today. His loving kindness keeps reaching out, so that every day we can begin again.

Jeremiah goes on to show that waiting and silence are also expressions of faith. In suffering, we do not rush to argue or escape, but choose to be quiet before the Lord, trusting his timing and his work. God does not delight in suffering, but he uses it to purify our hearts and teach us to rely on him in weakness. Though he brings grief, he does not cast off forever, and his compassion will in the end overcome all sorrow.
a: Remember the Lord’s loving kindness every day
Each morning remind yourself that God is still faithful and his grace is new every day.
Learn stillness in waiting
When circumstances are hard, learn to look up quietly. Do not respond from emotion, but trust God’s timing.
Believe his compassion never ceases
Even in suffering, be sure that God’s heart is gentle and his purpose is not to destroy but to shape and heal.
q: Can I still give thanks for God’s faithfulness in hard times? In seasons of waiting and pain, am I willing to choose quietness and trust?
pr: Lord, thank You that Your loving kindness never ends and Your faithfulness is new every morning. When I am weak or sorrowful, help me still to look to Your salvation. Help me to trust in the quiet and be strengthened in the waiting, for Your compassion never fails. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The Lord’s mercy is new every day, and I will find fresh strength in his faithfulness!

t: Drawn by Love, Gladly Following
v: The Song of songs, which is Solomon’s.
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth; for your love is better than wine.
Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is oil poured out, therefore the virgins love you.
Take me away with you. Let’s hurry. The king has brought me into his rooms. We will be glad and rejoice in you. We will praise your love more than wine! They are right to love you.
I am dark, but lovely, you daughters of Jerusalem, like Kedar’s tents, like Solomon’s curtains.
Don’t stare at me because I am dark, because the sun has scorched me. My mother’s sons were angry with me. They made me keeper of the vineyards. I haven’t kept my own vineyard.
b: The Song of Songs is not only a love poem; it is also a picture of the spiritual life. Here the bride represents a soul that loves the Lord and longs for him. She is drawn by the love of the bridegroom (who represents Christ) and is ready to run after him. Her prayer is: “Take me away with you. Let us hurry.” This is a life awakened by love and drawn on by grace.

Loving the Lord does not begin with effort; it begins with being drawn by his love. When we truly experience that his love is sweeter, purer, and more lasting than any joy in the world, longing grows naturally. The fragrance of that love, like precious oil, makes us want to draw near to him, know him, and follow him.

Yet the bride honestly admits her imperfection: “I am dark, but lovely.” These words hold a deep truth. Though we have sin, weakness, and the scars of the past, in the Lord’s eyes we are still seen as lovely, because his love covers us and makes us white as snow in his sight.

She also says, “They made me keeper of the vineyards. I haven’t kept my own vineyard.” This pictures how we are sometimes so busy with other things that we neglect our intimacy with the Lord. God wants more than our work for him. He wants us first to care for the “vineyard that is his,” our inner life of fellowship with him.
a: Let the Lord’s love draw you
Do not serve God out of duty or fear, but let his love set your heart on fire.
Be honest about yourself
Admit your darkness and shortcomings before the Lord, and he will restore your beauty with love.
Keep your vineyard
Do not let busyness steal your time with God. Enter his “inner room” every day.
q: Do I often neglect intimacy with the Lord because of busyness or service? Today, am I willing to be drawn by his love once again?
pr: Lord, thank You that Your love is better than wine and sweeter than life. Draw me once more, so that I run after You. Heal my heart that the sun has scorched, help me guard the inner vineyard, and in Your love let me recover the joy and beauty of life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am drawn by the Lord’s love and will run after him; though I am dark, I am lovely in his eyes!

t: The Cost and the Sweetness of True Discipleship
v: For I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste of my supper. For many are called, but few are chosen.’”
Now great multitudes were going with him. He turned and said to them,
“If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.
Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross and come after me, can’t be my disciple.
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation and isn’t able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build and wasn’t able to finish.’
Or what king, as he goes to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?
Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends an envoy and asks for conditions of peace.
So therefore, whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.
“Salt is good, but if the salt becomes flat and tasteless, with what do you season it?
It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile. It is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
b: In this passage Jesus reveals the true cost of being his disciple. He is not looking for crowds; he is looking for sincere hearts. Many followed him because they saw miracles, were fed, or wanted blessings, but Jesus turned and told them that to follow him they must be ready to give everything.

The Lord says, “If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t hate his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.” This does not mean we should not love our families; it means our love must be in order. Only when Christ is first will our love not be out of balance or tied up by emotion. Those who truly love the Lord also learn better how to love others with God’s love.

He also says, “Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross and come after me, can’t be my disciple.” The cross stands for self-denial and obedience. Everyone who follows the Lord must be willing to lay down their own rights, pride, and desires, learn to center their life on God’s will, and gladly take up the cross of living for him.

Jesus’ pictures of building a tower and going to war remind us that following him is not an impulse but a carefully considered commitment. True faith is not “just believe and that’s it,” but “believe and follow,” letting the whole life be changed by him.

Finally he says, “Salt is good, but if the salt becomes tasteless, it is useless.” Believers who lose their love and commitment to the Lord may keep an “outward form” but lose their spiritual flavor. Only when we are constantly renewed by the Lord’s love, so that our lives have saltiness and influence, can we live as true disciples.
a: Re-examine the order of your loves
Put Christ first in your life, and let no relationship or thing take his place.
Gladly take up your cross
Learn to lay down your pride, your ideas, and your need to control, and submit to God’s will.
Keep your spiritual saltiness
Stay close to the Lord and be renewed by his love, so that your life carries the flavor of the Kingdom of heaven.
q: Have I ever drawn back because the cost seemed too high? Am I willing to let the Lord’s love replace all my other motives, so that my faith is no longer an “add-on” but the foundation?
pr: Lord, You are worthy of my whole heart. Help me to stop centering on myself and to truly put You first. Whatever my circumstances, I am willing to take up my cross and follow You. Let my life always have heavenly saltiness and live in a way that glorifies You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am willing to pay the price, take up my cross, and truly follow the Lord Jesus, to be a disciple with salt and a witness!

t: Walking the Road of Righteousness and Honesty
v: No mischief shall happen to the righteous, but the wicked shall be filled with evil.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.
A prudent man keeps his knowledge, but the hearts of fools proclaim foolishness.
The hands of the diligent ones shall rule, but laziness ends in slave labor.
Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.
A righteous person is cautious in friendship, but the way of the wicked leads them astray.
The slothful man doesn’t roast his game, but the possessions of diligent men are prized.
In the way of righteousness is life; in its path there is no death.
b: This passage is like a picture of strong contrasts: the righteous and the wicked, honesty and lies, diligence and laziness, wisdom and foolishness. God uses it to remind us that the fruit of a life is often the accumulation of everyday choices.

First, God delights in those who “do the truth.” Honesty is not only telling the truth; it is an attitude of life that is real and without hypocrisy. An honest person does not cut corners, pretend, or cover up sin. Such a life pleases God and is kept by him. By contrast, lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, because lies come from fear and pride and destroy trust and relationships.

Second, Proverbs reminds us: “The hand of the diligent ruled, but the slothful will be put to forced labor.” Diligence is not only a work attitude; it is faithfulness to what God has entrusted to us. When we are diligent in small things and firm in faith, God lifts us up; laziness makes us miss opportunities and waste grace.

Third, a “kind word” can comfort a sorrowful heart. God wants our mouths to be full of gracious words that build people up rather than tear them down. Anxiety weighs a heart down, but a word from God can rekindle hope and set a soul on its feet again.

Finally, the passage ends with one summary: “In the way of righteousness is life. In its pathway there is no death.” Walking the road of righteousness is not always smooth, but it is the road that truly has life, because it leads in the end to eternal peace and glory.
a: Hold to honesty and truth
Even when the cost is high, do not trade lies for short-term gain.
Learn diligent faithfulness
Treat every day’s work and service as worship offered to God, and be faithful to what he has entrusted to you.
Be a person of kind words
Let your words be comfort and strength in others’ hearts, reflecting the love of Christ.
q: In my daily choices, am I walking the road of honesty, righteousness, and diligence? Do my words often carry the breath of life?
pr: Lord, let me walk in righteousness and honesty, and not be led astray by lies or laziness. Teach me to speak words that build people up, and to show Your glory in diligence. May my whole life walk in Your light and find the road that truly has life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will walk in honesty and righteousness, serve the Lord diligently, and let my life be full of light and the fragrance of life!

t: God’s Word Is Never Chained
v: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David, according to my Good News,
in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained.
Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
This saying is trustworthy: “For if we died with him, we will also live with him.
If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us.
If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.”
b: Paul wrote this letter from prison. His body was bound by chains, yet he declared, “The word of God isn’t chained!” These words are a firm hope for everyone who follows Christ. A person’s circumstances can be restricted, but the gospel cannot be locked up; a body can be imprisoned, but the truth of God can pass through walls and cross generations.

Paul reminds Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead.” This is not a religious slogan; it is the foundation of our faith. That Jesus rose from the dead proves that death, sin, and bondage cannot overcome him, and in him we are not overcome by hardship either.

Even when we suffer persecution, are misunderstood, or fall into difficulty, we can still have strength because of Christ’s resurrection. Paul says, “I endure all things for the sake of the chosen ones, that they also may obtain salvation.” He did not live for his own release; he endured so that others might receive eternal life. True love is willing to suffer for others.
Then he quotes a faithful saying, probably a hymn of the early church:
“If we died with him, we will also live with him. If we endure, we will also reign with him.”

This reminds us that believing in Christ is not an escape from pain; it is going through the cross with Christ and receiving resurrection life. God’s faithfulness does not depend on our steadiness. Even if we are weak or faithless, he does not change. He always keeps his covenant, because he cannot deny himself.
a: Remember the risen Lord
When you feel pressed or discouraged, think on Jesus’ resurrection and victory.
Endure in suffering
Do not be trapped by present limits. God is using your testimony to spread his word.
Hold on to faithfulness and hope: even in the dark, believe
that God’s word is never chained.
q: When you feel limited by circumstances or by people, do you still believe God’s word is at work? Are you willing to endure for the gospel so that others can see Christ through you?
pr: Lord, thank You that Your word is never chained. Even when I am trapped in hardship, Your truth moves freely. Give me a heart of endurance, so that I gladly pay the price for the gospel, and hold on to faith in weakness, testifying to Your unchanging faithfulness. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Though I am restricted, God’s word is not chained; I live with Christ and will overcome in him!

t: A Night of Tears, a Morning of Faith
v: Return, LORD. Deliver my soul, and save me for your loving kindness’ sake.
For in death there is no memory of you. In Sheol, who shall give you thanks?
I am weary with my groaning. Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.
My eye wastes away because of grief. It grows old because of all my adversaries.
Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard the voice of my weeping.
The LORD has heard my supplication. The LORD accepts my prayer.
May all my enemies be ashamed and dismayed. They shall turn back, they shall be disgraced suddenly.
b: This is a psalm that turns from despair to hope. David prays in extreme pain. He is worn out in body and spirit, his tears are like a river, and night after night he weeps, even saying, “I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.” It is the cry of a soul in deep distress, and it is the real struggle of a true spiritual life.

He is not complaining against God; he is honestly pouring out his heart to him. He knows that only God can turn and save. The focus of his prayer is not that God would remove the pain but that God would show mercy: “Save me for your loving kindness’ sake.” This line holds the core of faith: David’s hope is built not on circumstances but on God’s unchanging loving kindness.

As the psalm goes on, the turning point comes in verse 8: “The LORD has heard the voice of my weeping.” A heart that was full of tears begins to recover its faith. The pain does not vanish at once, but he is sure that God has heard. In that moment his tears become a prayer of faith, and the night of sorrow turns into a morning of trust.

At the end David declares, “All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed.” This is not pride; it is trust that God’s justice will be done. True victory is not the moment the enemy falls, but choosing, while you are still in tears, to believe that God’s loving kindness has not changed.
a: Pray honestly in pain
Do not hold back your tears. Let God be the one you weep to.
Choose to rely on God’s loving kindness
Even when you see no change, be sure that God’s love has not left you.
Declare faith in the midst of tears
Let prayer be the starting point of the turn, trusting that God has heard and will act.
q: Am I still grieving in the dark night? Am I willing to believe that God has already heard my cry?
pr: Loving Lord, You know the weariness and sorrow in my heart. Turn and save me, and let me remember Your loving kindness in my pain. Lord, thank You for hearing my weeping. Help me to trust You in my tears and to wait for Your salvation. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God has heard my cry, and his loving kindness will turn the night into morning!

t: A Body in Unity, Each Doing Its Part
v: For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.
For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
b: In this passage Paul shows that a believer’s life is not isolated; we are connected and complete one another. Christians are not lone believers; we belong to one body, the body of Christ.

First, Paul reminds us, “not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think.” Pride destroys unity and blinds us to the grace God has placed in others. Seeing ourselves with humility is the starting point of building unity, because each person’s gift, faith, and place are measured out by God; no one is higher and no one is lesser.

Then he uses the picture of a body: one body with many members, each different yet working together. The eye cannot replace the hand, and the hand cannot replace the foot. In the same way, God sets different gifts in the church to complete the function of the whole. If we value only our own role, we easily lose unity; only when we see the value of complementing one another can the church work in health.

Paul lists several gifts: prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, and mercy. These are not higher or lower positions but different directions of service. The point is not “what” we do but “how” we do it: • According to the proportion of faith: relying on God, not on our own strength. • Giving ourselves wholly: taking seriously what God has entrusted to us. • Liberality, diligence, and cheerfulness: living out an attitude of love in service.

When every member functions properly, the whole body shows the glory of Christ. Unity is not uniformity; it is being completed by one another in our differences. This is the beautiful mystery of the church.
a: Keep a humble heart
Do not think too highly of yourself or look down on others; respect what God is doing in each person.
Use the gifts God has given
Discover your gift and serve faithfully, so that God’s household is built up.
Build connection with one another
Do not walk alone or compare. Work together and complete one another in love.
q: Do I treasure and use the gifts God has given me? In the church, do I build others up in love rather than compare or criticize?
pr: Lord, thank You for making me a member of Your body. Teach me not to be proud or self-deprecating, but to serve humbly and give myself wholly to what You have entrusted to me. May my gifts be a blessing and make Your body one and glorify You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am a part of the body of Christ. I will faithfully use my gift and, together with all the members, build a glorious church!

t: My Help Comes from the Lord
v: I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?
My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber.
Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
The LORD is your keeper. The LORD is your shade on your right hand.
The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night.
The LORD will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul.
The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in, from this time forward, and forever more.
b: This Song of Ascents was sung by the Israelites as they went up to Jerusalem on pilgrimage. The journey was hard and the mountain roads ahead were dangerous. The psalmist lifted his eyes to the hills, not to seek help from the hills, but to look beyond them to the Lord who made them.

“My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.” This is a turning of faith from circumstances to the Creator. When we face challenges, we are quick to look to human help or our own ability, but the true source of strength is the God who never changes. He made heaven and earth, and he can surely hold you up for your whole life.

The psalmist uses the word “keep” again and again to stress God’s faithfulness and care. Unlike people, he does not grow tired, and unlike a night watchman, he does not doze; day and night he guards the people he loves. The sun by day and the moon by night stand for every danger, seen or hidden, and God protects you in all of them.

The last two verses carry the promise to its height: “The LORD will keep your soul. The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in, from this time forth, and forevermore.” God’s care is not limited by time or place. Wherever we are and whatever we face, we are kept in his hand.
a: Look to the Creator, not the circumstances
Do not only see the mountains and challenges before you. Fix your eyes on the God who made the mountains.
Trust that God’s keeping never slumbers
Whether in the toil of the day or the loneliness of the night, God is guarding you.
Rest in his eternal care
Your going out and coming in, your work, your family, and your future are all safe in his hand.
q: When I feel alone or helpless, who is the first one I look to? Do I believe God is watching over me day and night?
pr: Lord, my help comes from You, the Maker of heaven and earth. When I am weak, You hold me up; when I am afraid, You watch over me. Let me fix my eyes on Your faithfulness and trust Your keeping forever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth. He keeps me day and night, forever!

t: Offering the Costliest Love
v: Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.
So they made him a supper there. Martha served, but Lazarus was one of those who sat at the table with him.
Therefore Mary took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.
Then Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, one of his disciples, who would betray him, said,
“Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”
Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial.
For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me.”
b: This passage shows a beautiful and deep act of love. Mary understood that Jesus was about to go to the cross. She said nothing; she expressed her devotion to the Lord with her most precious ointment. That jar of pure nard was costly, worth about a year’s wages, yet she broke it without holding anything back and poured it on the Lord’s feet. It was a sign of complete surrender and worship.

The house was “filled with the fragrance of the ointment,” and it was more than a physical scent; it was the fragrance of love and offering. Mary’s act shows that she valued the Lord far above everything in the world. She did not wait until after the crucifixion to anoint his body; while he was still with her, she seized that unique moment with love.

Judas’ reaction, by contrast, shows coldness and selfishness. He used “caring for the poor” as an excuse, but there was no real love in his heart. The person who loves the Lord and the person who only counts profit are worlds apart. Jesus saw Mary’s heart and said, “Leave her alone.” He welcomes an offering that comes from true love.
Mary’s love was not rational calculation but spiritual understanding. She knew that Jesus’ cross was the beginning of salvation. Her act became a worship remembered forever in history.
a: Act in love without delay
Do not wait until it is too late to show your love for the Lord. Offer your most precious heart now.
Give your best to the Lord
Keep nothing back for yourself. Respond to his love with the fragrance of your life.
Let worship fill your life
When you love the Lord sincerely, the fragrance will naturally fill your home, your service, and your life.
q: What I give the Lord, is it leftover time and resources, or my most precious love? Does my worship give off a spiritual fragrance?
pr: Lord Jesus, You are worthy of all my love and devotion. Take away the calculating attitude in my heart, and let me, like Mary, respond to Your grace with the sincerest heart. May my life be a fragrant offering that glorifies Your name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will pour out the ointment of my life and offer my costliest love, and let the Lord’s fragrance fill my whole being!

t: A Testimony of Deliverance
v: They came to the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes.
When he had come out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit met him out of the tombs.
He lived in the tombs. Nobody could bind him any more, not even with chains,
because he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him, and the fetters broken in pieces. Nobody had the strength to tame him.
Always, night and day, in the tombs and in the mountains, he was crying out, and cutting himself with stones.
When he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and bowed down to him,
All the demons begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs, that we may enter into them.”
At once Jesus gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered into the pigs. The herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea, and they were drowned in the sea.
As he was entering into the boat, he who had been possessed by demons begged him that he might be with him.
He didn’t allow him, but said to him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.”
He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marveled.
b: Here was a man bound by darkness, abandoned by people, and cut off from society, yet Jesus came to the place where he was. No one could loosen his chains; only the Lord could set him free. This encounter shows the true meaning of salvation: Jesus does not wait for people to come looking for him; he walks into their despair.

The man’s possession pictures the condition of a person ruled by sin and fear: lonely, self-harming, hopeless, unable to control himself. Yet when he “saw Jesus from afar,” a faint awareness still drove him to run to the Lord. That one step changed everything. With one word from Jesus the unclean spirits left, and he was free. The man who had lost his dignity and lived among the tombs became a witness who proclaimed God’s grace.

The remarkable thing is that Jesus did not grant his request to be “with him,” but sent him home to be a witness. To truly walk with the Lord is not only to be at his side, but to testify for him in daily life. This is a mature faith: moving from being rescued to becoming a witness.
a: Let Jesus into your darkest places
He can set you free from every bondage that seems unsolvable.
Remember God’s mercy
He not only saves you from the past; he calls you back among people to live out a testimony.
Proclaim the Lord’s grace with your life
Your story may be where someone else’s hope begins.
q: Am I willing to let the Lord into the deepest pain and fear in my life? Can I, like this man, tell others of the Lord’s mercy?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for walking into the wasteland of my life to set me free and heal me. Keep me from living in the fear of the past, and make me a witness of Your grace, so that more people may see Your love through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I was once bound, but now I am free because of Jesus; I will testify to his mercy and power with my life!

t: Repent and Listen, and Escape the Discipline of Desolation
v: The LORD has sent to you all his servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them (but you have not listened or inclined your ear to hear),
saying, “Return now everyone from his evil way, and from the evil of your doings, and dwell in the land that the LORD has given to you and to your fathers, from of old and even forever more.
Don’t go after other gods to serve them or worship them, and don’t provoke me to anger with the work of your hands; then I will do you no harm.”
“Yet you have not listened to me,” says the LORD, “that you may provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own hurt.”
Therefore the LORD of Armies says: “Because you have not heard my words,

behold, I will send and take all the families of the north,” says the LORD, “and I will send to Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all these nations around. I will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and a hissing, and perpetual desolations.
Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp.
This whole land will be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
b: This passage reveals the tension between God’s call and human choice. God kept sending prophets, sincerely urging the people to turn from evil so that they could live in peace and receive blessing. But when the people repeatedly refused to listen, their rebellion led them to ruin. God’s discipline is not arbitrary revenge but a righteous response, meant to call hearts back and to warn the generations.

When people persist in unrepentance and worship other gods that God does not approve, they provoke him to anger by the choices of their own hands, and the discipline he allows comes upon them. Babylon becomes here the instrument God uses to warn. Its coming brings not only military defeat but desolation of social and spiritual life: the sound of wedding joy ends, daily work falls silent, and the rhythm of all life is broken.

For us today the warning is still real. The consequences of rebellion fall not only on individuals but also on families, churches, and nations. Repentance is not just a religious act; it is returning to the right relationship with God: being humble, turning from evil and doing good, and keeping a listening heart. When we are willing to incline our ear and respond, God’s blessing and peaceful dwelling can operate among us again.
a: Examine yourself and turn back regularly
Set aside time each day before the Lord, and when you find you have drifted, repent and turn back at once.
Refuse idols that take first place
Examine what in your life, made by your own hands (money, reputation, habits), has taken God’s place, and put the Lord first again.
Take spiritual responsibility for your community
In your family and church, be a voice that calls for repentance and obedience, and lay a foundation of blessing for the next generation.
q: Have I long ignored God’s reminders? Where do I need to turn back immediately and restore intimacy and obedience with God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, You rose early to send Your words calling us to return. Forgive us for our repeated disobedience. Give us humble hearts that incline our ears to You and turn back at once, away from everything that takes Your place. Make us and our families places fit to live in, kept from desolation, and let our lives and communities be a witness to Your grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I incline my ear to God and turn back at once; may he establish peace and lasting blessing in me and my family!

t: Ebenezer: Thus Far the LORD Has Helped Us
v: When the Philistines heard that the children of Israel were gathered together at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the children of Israel heard it, they were afraid of the Philistines.
The children of Israel said to Samuel, “Don’t stop crying to the LORD our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines.”
Samuel took a suckling lamb, and offered it for a whole burnt offering to the LORD. Samuel cried to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.

As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines came near to battle against Israel; but the LORD thundered with a great thunder on that day on the Philistines and confused them; and they were struck down before Israel.
The men of Israel went out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, and struck them until they came under Beth Kar.
Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
b: This passage records a decisive victory, won not by military strength but by God’s help. Israel had failed because of sin, but under Samuel’s leadership they repented, gathered, and cried out to God. When the enemy attacked again, they did not rely on themselves; they begged God to step in. This is the key to spiritual victory: when people humbly seek God, God fights for his people.

Samuel’s burnt offering stood for offering himself completely, an act of faith. At the very moment of the offering, the LORD himself “thundered with a mighty thunder.” It was not a tactic human hands could carry out; God himself acted, throwing the enemy army into confusion and defeat. This reminds us that real victory does not lie in our ability but in God’s presence and intervention.

After the battle Samuel set up a stone as a memorial and named it “Ebenezer,” which means “stone of help,” declaring, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” This is not only a look back at the past; it is confidence for the future. In our life of faith we also need such “markers” to remind ourselves that every step of keeping and every act of grace was the hand of God holding us up.
a: Choose to cry out to God in fear
When trouble comes, do not look first for methods; seek God’s intervention first.
Respond to crisis with faith
Like Samuel, replace anxiety and escape with worship and offering.
Set up spiritual markers
Record God’s help (in notes, a prayer journal, a stone of thanks), and often look back on “thus far the LORD has helped me.”
q: Am I still facing challenges with my own methods? What are the things I need to declare again: “Lord, thus far You have helped me”?
pr: Lord, You are my stone of help, the God of Ebenezer. When I face fear and battle, teach me not to rely on myself but to turn wholly to You. Thank You for every rescue and guidance in the past. I will set up a stone of remembrance and declare Your faithfulness forever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Thus far the LORD has helped me! He is the strength of my victory, the Ebenezer of my whole life!

t: Laying the Foundation Again: Glory Restored in Worship
v: When the seventh month had come, and the children of Israel were in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem.
They kept the feast of booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number, according to the ordinance, as the duty of every day required;

and afterward the continual burnt offering, the offerings of the new moons, of all the set feasts of the LORD that were consecrated, and of everyone who willingly offered a free will offering to the LORD.
From the first day of the seventh month, they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD; but the foundation of the LORD’s temple was not yet laid.

Then Jeshua stood with his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together to have the oversight of the workmen in God’s house: the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brothers the Levites.

When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD’s temple, they set the priests in their vestments with trumpets, with the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel.

They sang to one another in praising and giving thanks to the LORD, “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever toward Israel.” All the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the LORD’s house had been laid.
b: After seventy years in exile, the Israelites had finally returned to their land. The surroundings were still in ruins and the temple had not been rebuilt, yet the first thing they did was not build walls or settle homes; they gathered “as one man” to worship God. It is a deeply moving picture: at the start of rebuilding, they made worship the foundation.

The people kept the feast, offered sacrifices, and praised together, showing that they understood that the key to revival is restoring the relationship with God. True rebuilding is not outward construction but the renewal of the spiritual foundation. At the moment the builders laid the temple’s foundation, the priests blew trumpets, the Levites clashed cymbals, and all the people praised loudly: “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever toward Israel!” This was a spiritual declaration: however much was destroyed in the past, God’s loving kindness has not changed.

Our lives today need this kind of rebuilding too. When our faith, family, or ministry seems shattered, God calls us first to restore “the foundation of worship.” Praise is not the result of rebuilding; it is the beginning of it. When we choose to worship in the midst of chaos, God’s glory appears again.
a: Worship first, then rebuild
In the midst of problems, return first to God and let him be the center again.
Worship in unity
Gather with brothers and sisters in praise. Spiritual unity is where God’s power begins to work.
Declare faith in praise
Even if circumstances are still broken, declare, “He is good, and his loving kindness endures forever.”
q: Have I made worship the foundation of my life? When I face rebuilding and challenges, is my first step to look to God or to rely on myself?
pr: Dear Lord, thank You for showing grace even in the ruins. Restore the altar in my heart, so that I worship You first and then do anything else. Let my praise be the new foundation, and let Your glory be established in my life again. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I choose worship as my foundation! Even though circumstances are not yet fully restored, I declare: the LORD is good, and his loving kindness toward me endures forever!

t: Walking in the Way You Should Go
v: A good name is more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold.
The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is the maker of them all.
A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.
The result of humility and the fear of the LORD is wealth, honor, and life.
Thorns and snares are in the path of the wicked; whoever guards his soul stays far from them.
Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.
b: This passage is a portrait of the wise life. From how we live to how we act to how we raise our children, everything centers on “the fear of the Lord.” Scripture reminds us that true blessing is not measured by how much wealth we have, but by whether we walk the right path that God has set.

“A good name is more desirable than great riches.” Character is worth far more than silver and gold. Wealth may attract people for a while, but a good name and an upright life are treasures God values and that never lose their shine.

“A prudent man sees danger and hides himself.” Wisdom is not running from responsibility. It is knowing how to discern the times in the light of God and to stay away from evil paths. The foolish act on impulse and end up trapped. True wisdom comes from fearing God and walking in humility, because “the reward of humility and the fear of the Lord is riches, honor, and life.”

The last verse is a truth many parents know well: “Train up a child in the way he should go, and even when he is old he will not depart from it.” This is not an education formula but a spiritual principle. When parents turn a child’s heart toward God from an early age and help him know the truth and fear the Lord, that foundation sinks deep and becomes the direction of a whole lifetime.
a: Seek to honor God’s name
more than earthly gain and achievement.
Practice reverence and humility every day
so that you find favor with God and honor among people.
Raise the next generation
by your own example, passing on a faith that fears the Lord.
q: Do I care more about how God sees me than how people judge me? Am I living out reverence and humility as an example at home and at work?
pr: Lord, teach me to walk in the way I should go. Keep me from being deceived by riches or becoming proud in success. Let me be blessed in reverence and find life in humility, and let me be an example of faith to the next generation. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I choose to fear God and walk an upright path. The Lord will give me honor and life, and my family will walk in his ways from generation to generation!

t: Treasuring the Knowledge of Christ Above All
v: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord! To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not tiresome, but for you it is safe.
Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the false circumcision.
For we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh;
though I myself might have confidence even in the flesh. If any other man thinks that he has confidence in the flesh, I yet more:
circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee;
concerning zeal, persecuting the assembly; concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless.
However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith,
b: Paul wrote these words from prison, yet he did not pity himself or complain. Instead he declared with great joy, “I count all things to be loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.” This sentence opens up the heart of the spiritual life: true joy lies not in what we have, but in whom we know.

Paul once had every reason to boast: a noble birth, a blameless record under the law, and boundless zeal. But when he met Christ, everything people consider glorious became “refuse.” Only Christ has eternal worth. Paul knew that having “no confidence in the flesh” is true freedom. It means not relying on outward credentials or religious performance, but trusting in Christ by faith.

“The righteousness which is from God by faith” means it is not about what we do for God, but about all that Christ has accomplished for us. When we understand this, we can be like Paul, no longer shaken by outward success or failure, and able to rejoice in the Lord alone.
a: Let go of worldly boasting
and shift the center of what you truly value to Christ.
Rejoice in the Lord in every circumstance
not because of your situation, but because you are “in the Lord.”
Reflect often
Am I pursuing Christ himself, or what he can give me?
q: What are the things I think are “gain” that are actually keeping me from knowing Christ more deeply? Am I willing to let them go in order to gain him?
pr: Lord Jesus, You are the most precious treasure of my life. Help me to count all things as loss and to boast only in knowing You. Let my heart stop relying on achievement or performance, and find the joy of freedom simply by trusting in You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I treasure the knowledge of Christ above all! I do not boast in the flesh. I rejoice only in the Lord’s grace, and through him I have found the truest life!

t: Strong in Weakness
v: I know a man in Christ who was caught up into the third heaven fourteen years ago—whether in the body, I don’t know, or whether out of the body, I don’t know; God knows.
I know such a man (whether in the body, or outside of the body, I don’t know; God knows),
how he was caught up into Paradise and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.
For if I would desire to boast, I will not be foolish; for I will speak the truth. But I refrain, so that no man may think more of me than that which he sees in me or hears from me.

By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, a thorn in the flesh was given to me: a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively.
Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me.
He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.
Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.
b: Paul’s testimony here shows what spiritual maturity looks like. He had once received revelations of the highest order, even being caught up to the “third heaven” and hearing the secrets of Paradise. Yet he did not boast about that glorious experience. He boasted about his weakness instead. He understood that spiritual power does not come from the mountaintop experiences people have, but from depending on God’s grace.

That “thorn in the flesh” may have been an illness, persecution, or an emotional burden. Scripture does not say, because the point is not the kind of thorn but its purpose: to keep him from being exalted and to teach him to depend on God. Paul begged the Lord three times to take the pain away, and he heard the Lord’s gentle but firm answer: “My grace is sufficient for you.” These words have strengthened believers in every generation.

The Lord did not grant his request to “remove the thorn,” but gave him the strength to “bear the thorn.” True strength is not the absence of weakness, but grace holding us up within it. When we admit our limits, God’s power comes, and his glory shines through our brokenness.
a: Do not run from weakness
It is the very place where God wants to display his grace.
Learn to depend on him in hardship
Ask not for the pain to be removed at once, but for his power to rest on you.
Give the glory to God
When people see your endurance and joy, they will see Christ in you.
q: Am I still complaining to God about the “thorns” in my life? Am I willing to believe they are exactly what makes me depend more on his grace?
pr: Lord, thank You that Your grace is sufficient for me. When I am weak, let Your power rest on me so that I no longer rely on myself. Teach me to trust You even in pain, for I know that Your power is made perfect in my weakness. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I no longer fear weakness, because the Lord’s grace is sufficient for me! His power rests on me, so I am strong in weakness and victorious in difficulty!

t: A Life Walking with God
v: Enoch lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Methuselah.
After Methuselah’s birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
All the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years.
Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
b: In a generation where human hearts were corrupt and evil was spreading, Scripture still takes care to record Enoch’s name. It was not for any outstanding achievement, but because he “walked with God.” These four words are the deepest core of the life of faith: not working for God, but walking with God.

Enoch was not a hermit who withdrew from others. He “had other sons and daughters” and lived an everyday life, yet in ordinary days he chose to walk every step with God. That means his life, his thoughts, and his choices were all lived in God’s presence. He did not draw near to God only now and then. He walked with him for three hundred years, day after day.

“God took him” suggests he was taken up without experiencing death. It is a spiritual picture: those who walk with God are already joined to eternity. Walking with God is not a moment of passion but a lifetime of commitment; not an outward show but inner intimacy with God.
a: Set aside time each day to walk with God, whether in prayer, reflection, walking, or stillness.
Look for God’s presence in everyday matters, and let him be the center of your life.
Replace your own opinions with obedience, and line up every step of your life with the Lord.
q: Is my faith only Sunday worship, or do I walk with God every day? In the busyness of life, do I still keep room to walk with the Lord?
pr: Lord, I long to walk with You every day as Enoch did. Teach me to know You and draw near to You in ordinary life. Let my heart talk with You all the time, and let my steps follow Your leading. May my whole life be used by You and accepted by You, a life that walks with You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I choose to walk with God, not by feelings and not by circumstances. Because he is with me, my life is full of peace and eternal hope!

t: In the Body of Christ, Each in Our Role, Building One Another Up
v: For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.
For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
b: Paul first reminds us that every gift and every place comes from God, so serving begins with thinking “soberly.” We are neither proud nor self-belittling, because God gives each person a different role according to a measure of faith. Humility is returning to our rightful place: acknowledging that the Lord is King and that I am only one part of his body.

Then he uses the body as a picture of Christ’s church. Every member matters, and each has a function no one else can fill. God does not want us to become someone else. He wants us to offer the part he has given us. The hand cannot replace the foot, and the eye cannot stand in for the ear; when every member works faithfully, the whole body is healthy and strong. This is the beauty of God’s divine order: complementing one another and building one another up.

Finally, Paul shows that the heart of spiritual service is not gifting but love. Love is sincere, practical, and concrete. Love can walk with others and embrace both their joy and their tears; love brings out fervent service and gives us endurance in trouble and steadfastness in prayer. When the love of Christ flows among us, the body is built up, and Jesus receives all the glory.
a: Be faithful with the gift God has given you
Do not envy another’s place or despise your own. Where you are is where God most wants to use you.
Appreciate each other’s different graces and build one another up
Stop comparing and start appreciating. When you bless others, the whole body is lifted together.
Link with one another through sincere love
Walk together in love: care, accompany, and share burdens, so that Christ’s life flows among you and builds God’s unity.
q: Am I willing to serve faithfully in the place God has given me, and to build up every member around me with sincere love?
pr: Lord Jesus, give me a humble heart, that I may know my place and joyfully use the gift You have given me. Place sincere love within me, so that I can appreciate every brother and sister and build them up, and so that Your body is built up in love and all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will serve faithfully in the body of Christ and build others up with love!

t: Let Your Tongue Be a Tree of Life, Not a Wounding Blade
v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.
Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!
The path of life leads upward for the wise, to keep him from going downward to Sheol.
The LORD will uproot the house of the proud, but he will keep the widow’s borders intact.
The LORD detests the thoughts of the wicked, but the thoughts of the pure are pleasing.
He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but he who hates bribes will live.
The heart of the righteous weighs answers, but the mouth of the wicked gushes out evil.
b: Scripture reminds us of the power of the tongue, and Proverbs goes deeper: the tongue is not neutral. It will either be a tree of life or a blade that destroys. The first passage shows how “gentleness” can quiet fierce anger, while harsh words are like a match that easily sets conflict ablaze. A truly gentle tongue comes from a heart that submits to the Lord, that does not rely on self, struggle for power, or act out of pride. This is the life of selflessness: let Jesus be King, and let the Holy Spirit lead the tongue so that words bring healing.

The second passage points to the beauty of “a word in season.” Words led by the Holy Spirit are always timely, fitting, and true. The wise do not answer quickly. They think first, listen first, and wait first. The righteous can build people up with their mouths because they have first been renewed within by God’s Word. Here life beats technique and the heart beats method; a clean spring naturally gives clear water.

Finally, Proverbs reminds us that God watches all our words and thoughts. Pride, evil schemes, and greed all find their way into what we say; but love, grace, and purity can also show in our words. Words are a mirror of the heart, and the mouth lets us see whether we are really depending on the Lord or on our own flesh. When a person lets Jesus rule, his tongue bears the fruit of life, bringing comfort, direction, and support to others.
a: Answer gently instead of striking back with emotion
When conflict comes, pause and pray one line: “Lord, take charge of my tongue.” A gentle answer is not weakness; it is the power of the Holy Spirit.
Think before you speak, and start from love
Ask yourself three things: Is it true? Is it helpful? Is it timely? If it will not build up, choose silence.
Let your tongue be a tree of life
Deliberately feed the people around you with words of affirmation, thanks, blessing, and encouragement, and let your mouth be a channel of God’s grace.
q: Do my words give people life, or do they wound them? Am I willing to let the Lord take charge of my tongue?
pr: Lord Jesus, cleanse my mouth and renew my heart, so that my tongue no longer speaks from the flesh but from Your life. Fill me with Your love, that I may answer with gentleness, reply with wisdom, and build people up with grace, and let my mouth be a tree of life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: In Christ, my tongue will be a tree of life, bringing healing and blessing!

t: Affliction Brings Me Back to the Sweetness of God’s Word
v: You have treated your servant well, according to your word, LORD.
Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in your commandments.
Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I observe your word.
You are good, and do good. Teach me your statutes.
The proud have smeared a lie upon me. With my whole heart, I will keep your precepts.
Their heart is as callous as the fat, but I delight in your law.
It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.
The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.
b: The psalmist speaks with great honesty about his walk with God. He begins by acknowledging that God has always dealt well with his servant according to his word. God’s goodness is not an accident but his very nature. Every word he speaks and every deed he does carries healing and guidance.

The psalmist also confesses his own weakness frankly: “Before I was afflicted, I went astray.” Affliction is not God’s malice but a reminder of his tender love, turning us from our own center back to God’s way. Pain is like a mirror that shows our pride, our straying, and our blindness, and makes us hunger for his truth again.

Facing attacks, lies, and misunderstanding, he did not let emotion pull him along. He resolved to focus on God’s precepts. He was not carried away by what people said, but let God’s Word be his focus. Those people’s hearts were “as callous as fat,” dull and unfeeling, but he loved God’s law all the more, because only God’s Word can keep the heart awake and tender and keep it from falling into the trap of human conflict.

The psalmist even reaches a profound conclusion: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted.” Affliction let him know God more deeply and learn his heart, and it showed him that God’s Word is more real and more valuable than all the gold and silver in the world.
a: Seek God more deeply in hard times
Do not rush to complain or escape. Quietly ask the Lord, “What do you want me to learn on this road?”
Guard your heart with God’s Word in the face of criticism and lies
Do not let human voices rise above God’s voice. Choose to keep the Lord’s Word with your whole heart.
Value God’s Word above the world’s benefits
Set a regular time to read Scripture and think on the truth, and let God’s Word become the treasure of your heart.
q: What afflictions have taught me the deepest lessons from God’s Word?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for showing me grace even in hard times. Help me to love Your Word more in trials, to stand firm in Your truth and not be shaken by the lies of others. May Your Word be the most precious inheritance of my whole life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The Lord’s Word is more precious than gold and silver, an eternal strength in my heart!

t: Faith Is the Eye That Sees the Unseen
v: Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.
For by this, the elders obtained approval.
By faith we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible.

By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he had testimony given to him that he was righteous, God testifying with respect to his gifts; and through it he, being dead, still speaks.
b: Faith is first described as “assurance” and “proof.” It is not optimism based on feelings or blind imagination, but trust that stands on God’s Word. When God said, “Let there be light,” there was light; faith is believing that his Word is more real than our present circumstances. Those who walk by sight look at circumstances; those who walk by faith hold on to what God has said. When the heart is fixed on the Lord, the Holy Spirit leads us, and we no longer rely on ourselves but on the One who rules over all.

The passage also reminds us that the elders obtained a good testimony by faith. Their lives were not free of storms, but in the storms they chose to depend on God. By faith we know the world was created by God’s Word, and that keeps us from being swallowed up by difficulty and lets us see hope in the dark. Faith turns us from an earthly viewpoint to heaven’s, from the temporary to the eternal, from relying on ourselves to depending on God.

Abel’s story shows us that true faith overflows into worship and giving. His offering was accepted by God, not because it cost more outwardly, but because his heart was pure, selfless, and turned toward God alone. Even after his death, his life still speaks: true worship is not a single act but a lifelong attitude. When we put Jesus first, humbly obey, and follow the Holy Spirit with our hearts, the life we offer is a sacrifice with a fragrance God delights in.
a: See difficulty through faith
Ask yourself: Is what I face a limit, or the starting point of something new God is doing? Listen for the Lord’s voice with your heart, and you will not be led by fear.
Let God’s Word be your most reliable foundation
Keep God’s Word in your heart every day. Let his truth be a lamp to your feet, better than acting from the flesh.
Stay selfless in worship and service
Like Abel, live not for yourself or for appearances, but for the Lord alone. When your heart is fixed on Jesus, you will live a life that glorifies him.
q: In today’s challenges, am I relying on my own judgment, or letting faith lead me toward God’s will?
pr: Lord Jesus, give me faith that comes from heaven, so that I will still trust You in the unknown and still see hope in the dark. Help me not to be swayed by circumstances, but to hold fast to Your Word with my heart. Cleanse my heart too, so that I may offer a life that pleases You and live out the fragrance of true worship. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I walk by faith, not by sight, and I will see the Lord’s work!

t: Hold Fast to the Truth and Leave No Opening
v: You were running well! Who interfered with you that you should not obey the truth?
This persuasion is not from him who calls you.
A little yeast grows through the whole lump.
I have confidence toward you in the Lord that you will think no other way. But he who troubles you will bear his judgment, whoever he is.
b: Paul says, “You were running well!” It is a reminder spoken with a hurting heart. People who were walking in the truth, how did they suddenly get hindered? The life of faith is not just about starting well; it is about staying fixed on the Lord. Often what stops us is not a huge temptation but a small drift: one wrong voice, one twisted mindset, one unresolved emotion. These can turn us from focusing on Jesus to following other voices. True obedience is selflessness, with Jesus as the focus. It means listening not to those who seem zealous, but to the Lord who called us.

Paul warns, “A little yeast leavens the whole lump.” Yeast pictures wrong teaching, a proud heart, or self-centeredness. A little pride brings great corruption; a trace of self can spoil a whole life; a bit of wrong values can disturb an entire church. So Paul stresses staying alert and giving the enemy no foothold. When we live in the Spirit, return to the truth, and let Jesus be King, our lives stay pure.

Finally, Paul says, “I have confidence toward you in the Lord that you will think no other way.” This is a pastor’s confidence, and the hope Christians have for one another. It is not by human strength but by the Lord’s grace that we can return to the right path. Paul also points out that those who trouble the church will bear their own judgment. God is just, and he will deal with all who disturb the truth; our part is to focus on following the Lord and not be shaken. Follow the Lord with the heart and we are made firm; rely on ourselves with the mind and we are thrown into confusion. True victory is not striking back but standing firm in Christ.
a: Check your life for “a little yeast”
Think: Is there a small pride, a small grudge, or a small indulgence in me that I have not dealt with? These affect the whole spiritual life.
Listen to the Lord’s voice, not the voices that hinder
Do not be carried away by human enthusiasm, theories, or pressure. Simply ask, “Is this the Lord’s voice?” Let Jesus be King.
Run the whole race with determination
Faith is not a sprint. Returning each day to the truth, the Spirit, and Jesus is the strength to keep running.
q: Is there a seemingly small “yeast” in my life that is quietly hindering me from obeying the truth?
pr: Lord Jesus, keep my heart fixed on You alone, so that no voice hinders me from running the heavenly road. Shine on the “little yeast” in my life, and make me willing to be humble, repent, and be made pure again. Let me run without growing weary by the Holy Spirit, hold fast to the truth, and follow You to the end. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will hold fast to the truth and give the enemy no opening!

t: In the Wilderness, Meeting the God Who Sees Me
v: Sarai said to Abram, “This wrong is your fault. I gave my servant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised me. May the LORD judge between me and you.”
But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
The LORD’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur.
He said, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?” She said, “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
The LORD’s angel said to her, “Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.”
The LORD’s angel said to her, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, that they will not be counted for multitude.”
The LORD’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has heard your affliction.
He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him. He will live opposed to all of his brothers.”
She called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?”
b: Hagar’s story is full of tears and loneliness. She was not a main figure in the family, only a servant, yet she was caught up in the weakness of Abram and Sarai. Used, looked down on, and mistreated, she was so heartbroken that she could only flee into the wilderness. People saw her as expendable, but God had not forgotten her. When she was most alone, most helpless, and out of options, God came to find her himself.

The angel of the Lord asked Hagar, “Where did you come from? Where are you going?” It was not that God did not know. He was gently inviting her to face the truth and return to his light. People run away because they are afraid, but God seeks us in order to heal us. God did not only call her to go back; he also gave her a promise: he had heard her affliction and would make a way for her. God’s response was not rebuke but grace.

So Hagar said, “You are a God who sees.” In human eyes she was lowly, but in God’s eyes she was seen, heard, and remembered. Though humble in status, she became the first person to give God a name, because she had experienced him herself. Many times we think we are overlooked by people, pressed down by circumstances, or driven into the wilderness by problems, but God is right there waiting for us. He sees us and hears us, and he prepares grace to lead us back into his purpose.
a: Receive God’s call in the wilderness
Do not look only at how hard things are. Ask yourself, “What is God saying to me here?” He often speaks to us in the loneliest places.
Believe that God sees everything about you
People may overlook you, misunderstand you, or even mistreat you, but God has never taken his eyes off you. He sees your tears and hears your sighs.
Return to the place where God wants you to stand
Sometimes running away is not the answer; obedience is the way out. Go back to where God wants you, and he will walk with you and open the way.
q: Am I willing to stop in the wilderness and hear God’s gentle call to me?
pr: Lord who sees me, I give You my loneliness, my hurt, and my feeling of being misunderstood. Help me see that Your eyes are always on me, so that I stop running away and return to Your will and Your way. May Your grace sustain me, and let me experience Your presence even in hardship. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: In the wilderness, God sees me, and God leads me!
